gear: sun protection (south/southeast aspect, little shade above treeline)

before.overview: Mount Ellinor (5,944 ft) is one of the most popular and heavily trafficked summits in the southeastern Olympics, on Trail #812 in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness of Olympic National Forest, rising directly above Lake Cushman. The trail climbs through old-growth forest into open subalpine parkland to a narrow summit ridge with sweeping views of Lake Cushman, Hood Canal, the Kitsap Peninsula, and — on clear days — Mount Rainier and neighboring Mount Washington and The Brothers. The mountain is best known regionally for its long, sun-exposed spring snow chute, one of the most reliable early-season glissades in the Olympics, and for the crowds it draws on summer weekends given its short approach relative to the payoff.
before.beta: From the upper trailhead the trail climbs almost immediately via stacked switchbacks for about 0.3 mile before merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. From there it continues at a steady, 'character-building' grade through forest, breaks out of the trees into rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows, passes through a notch, and finishes with a short scramble to the true summit. It is a non-technical trail/scramble (no rope or rack needed in summer conditions) but is consistently steep with minimal flat ground. This is the standard, most direct route; a longer alternative starts from the lower trailhead (2,600 ft, no fee) and joins the same trail at the 3,900 ft merge point.
before.turnaround: Because the upper mountain is open, south-facing, and offers little shelter or route-finding cues in cloud, set a turnaround time that gets you off the exposed chute and summit basin before afternoon thunderstorms, wind, or fog move in, and before early-season snow softens into avalanche-prone slush.
before.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent Interagency/America the Beautiful pass) required to park at the upper trailhead; no separate wilderness permit needed for this day hike.
before.descent: Descend the same trail. In early season (roughly April–June) the snow-filled chute below the summit basin is commonly glissaded, but it is a southeast-facing, sun-exposed avalanche funnel that can turn to wet-slide hazard by early-mid afternoon — go early, check NWAC, and carry/know how to self-arrest with an ice axe. The rocks bordering the chute are extremely slick when wet or foggy.
obj_haz: Seasonal snow/avalanche chute (winter line) with fall/avalanche risk into early summer
Slick wet rock near the summit notch

pro_tips: Start early on weekends — Ellinor is one of the most crowded trails in the Olympics and the upper-trailhead lot fills fast
No water sources on route; carry all you need, especially across the sun-exposed upper slopes
In spring, check NWAC and recent trip reports before glissading the chute — it's a sun-exposed avalanche funnel that softens fast by afternoon
The lower and upper trailhead trails merge around 3,900 ft, so hiking up one and down the other is an option with a shuttle vehicle
watch_out: Rocks lining the summer chute are extremely slick when wet or foggy (official USFS warning)
Kicked-loose rock from parties above on the popular chute
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes — stay on the established path
before.best_season: The upper trailhead and access road are open early summer through fall (roughly June–October); the lower, fee-free trailhead can often be reached earlier in spring. The snow chute is a classic glissade objective April–June while it still holds continuous snow — check NWAC advisories and recent trip reports, since the chute is an avalanche funnel that gets sun-baked by early-mid afternoon.
before.approach: From the Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24/FS 2419 — the lot has a vault toilet, picnic table, and requires a Northwest Forest Pass), Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is a set of stacked, stairstep switchbacks gaining steadily through forest before the upper-trailhead route merges with the longer lower-trailhead trail (2,600 ft TH, 3.1 mi one-way) at roughly 3,900 ft. From the junction, continue up along the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline (~4,500 ft) around 1 mile in. Here is a well-signed junction where the winter/climbers' route breaks right up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, while the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, many switchbacks having stairstep risers that add to the grade. In summer conditions (roughly July–October) the trail is snow-free and well-cut essentially to the top, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes before the final approach to the 5,944 ft summit — total gain from the Upper TH is 2,444 ft over 1.6 mi one-way. There is no reliable water source on the upper route; carry all the water you need. Outside of core summer (roughly November–June), snow typically fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties climb the chute directly instead of the buried summer trail — this demands an ice axe and traction devices (crampons/microspikes), and the terrain is a steep, funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check avalanche conditions before heading up, and note that rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside of full winter conditions.
before.descent_text: Descend Trail #812 back to the Upper Trailhead — this is a hike/scramble with a walk-down descent and no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels, no technical anchors involved). When the upper mountain still holds a firm, continuous snowpack in the chute (common well into early summer most years), the popular and much faster descent line leaves the summer switchbacks and drops directly down the chute below the summit saddle: with an ice axe carried in self-arrest position, this is a well-known glissade losing roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes, with glissaders reportedly hitting 10+ mph on good snow. This is genuinely consequential terrain, not a casual slide — an uncontrolled or involuntary glissade, a fall on hard/icy snow without self-arrest skill, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute can cause serious injury, so only glissade in full control and bail to the trail if conditions look icy, rocky, or overly fast. Later in the season, as snow in the chute thins and exposes talus and rock, glissading becomes dangerous rather than fun, and the correct call is to stay on the maintained summer switchbacks for the entire descent. Whichever line is taken above timberline, the two rejoin at the signed timberline junction around 4,500 ft. The next junction below that, at roughly 3,900 ft, is a different one and works the other way: it is where the longer lower-trailhead trail splits off, and it is the recorded spot where parties descend to the wrong trailhead, so stay on the upper-trailhead branch there unless you deliberately left a shuttle car at the lower lot. From that merge it is a straightforward 0.3-mile drop down the stacked switchbacks back to the Upper Trailhead parking area.
before.bail: Turn around on the trail at any point; the snow chute is the main committing section in spring.

pitch_detail.notes: Stacked switchbacks climbing steeply through forest for ~0.3 mi, from 3,500 ft to the ~3,900 ft junction with the lower trailhead trail.
Trail breaks into open rock-strewn slopes and gravelly alpine meadows; follows the historic avalanche chute line in winter.
Short final scramble through a notch to the summit; loose rock and exposure reported by climbers; the crux of the route in terms of footing.

itinerary.cal: Snow commonly lingers in the summit chute into June; an ice axe and microspikes/crampons are the norm for spring ascents, while the dry summer trail (no supplemental gear) is typical by mid-to-late July.

days.note: A short, steep half-day outing from the Upper Trailhead (NFR 24): trail climbs through timber, breaks into rocky meadows and a notch, then a rocky scramble to the open summit with Olympic and Puget Sound views. Most parties are up and down in 3.5-5 hours including a summit break; no camping or overnight gear needed.

access.fees: $5/vehicle day-use fee or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the upper trailhead — pay via the on-site Scan & Pay/fee machine or display a valid Interagency/Digital Pass (cash not accepted on site). The lower trailhead is fee-free.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — the only charge is the Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent recreation pass) for parking at the upper trailhead.
access.rules: This is a car-to-car day scramble with no camping — no NPS wilderness-permit or bear-canister rules apply here. Standard Olympic National Forest day-use etiquette (Leave No Trace, stay on the boot path) applies.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent Interagency/America the Beautiful pass) required only for upper-trailhead parking; no wilderness permit needed for day hiking.
access.closures: FS Road 2419/2419-014 is gated and snow-covered in winter and early spring; the upper trailhead is open from early summer through fall. Check the Olympic National Forest alerts page for current road washouts or closures before driving up.

climate.typical: Drier southeastern-Olympic climate, but the steep south-facing chute can stay snowy well into early summer.

bySeason.spring: Upper chute holds firm snow; classic snow climb / glissade with ice axe.
bySeason.summer: Dry Class 2 hiking trail; best for hikers.
bySeason.winter: Full winter conditions; the road and upper trailhead are typically snowbound.

emergency.notes: Hoodsport Family Clinic (primary/urgent care), about 9 mi south of the SR 119 junction on US 101, is closer for non-emergency issues.
emergency.rangerStation: Hood Canal Ranger District, Olympic National Forest — office at 295142 US-101 S, Quilcene, WA 98376, (360) 765-2200 (the former Hoodsport office closed in 2005)

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends year-round when accessible, heaviest May-June (glissade season) and July-August (dry-trail hiking season); trip reports consistently flag both trailheads as tight/overflowing by mid-morning on weekends.
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very high — one of the most heavily-trafficked scrambles in the Olympics. Likely several hundred to 1,000+ parties over a summer season, with the spring snow-climb/glissade window drawing especially large weekend crowds.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate but short — about 2,400 ft of gain over ~1.6 mi one way (steep, sustained grade); most parties complete the round trip in 3-5 hours, so this suits partners who want a hard half-day rather than an all-day fitness test.
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light daypack (roughly 15-20 lb) — water, layers, and in spring an ice axe plus optionally microspikes/traction; no overnight or technical gear needed.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Short — trailhead is reached by car (NFR 24) and the climb itself is only ~1.6 mi one way to the summit, so total car-to-car time is typically a half day.
requiredSkills: Ice axe self-arrest and glissade control for the Apr-Jun snow-gully route
Basic Class 2-3 scrambling movement on rock/talus
Route-finding when the trail is snow-covered in shoulder season
Comfort sharing a popular trail/chute with many other parties (kicked-loose rock awareness)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Beginner-friendly for the dry-season (Jul-Oct) Class 2 hike; intermediate scrambler for the Apr-Jun snow-climb variation, since a partner needs to be comfortable on steep, firm snow with real runout consequences and confident self-arresting rather than learning it here.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July-October for the dry Class 2 hiking trail; late April-June for the classic firm-snow climb and glissade in the upper chute.

May.reason: Classic snow-climb and glissade season in the upper chute; very popular weekend window, ice axe required.

July.reason: Dry Class 2 trail is generally established; best conditions for straightforward hiking.

June.reason: Transitional — snow in the chute is softening and patchier; trail may be snow-covered in spots making route-finding harder.

April.reason: Upper chute typically still holds firm, steep snow suited to an early-season snow climb, but avalanche/firm-snow fall hazard is at its highest and the road/lower approach can still be snow-affected.

August.reason: Peak dry-trail hiking conditions and peak crowding.

October.reason: Still within the dry hiking window, but early snow is possible late in the month.

September.reason: Dry trail continues; crowds ease slightly after summer peak.

November-March.reason: Outside the best-season; road and upper trailhead are typically snowbound with full winter conditions.

weather.typical: Drier southeastern-Olympic microclimate, but the steep south/southeast-facing chute holds firm snow well into early summer even when the surrounding area is dry.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Primary risk is a fall on the steep, firm early-season snow in the upper chute, which can turn into a long, fast glissade/slide with rocks in the runout; secondary exposure is kicked-loose rock from the many parties above on this very popular route, and getting off-route onto steeper terrain if the trail is snow-covered.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24/FS 2419 - the lot has a vault toilet, picnic table, and requires a Northwest Forest Pass), Trail #812 climbs immediately.

before.rope_note: Standard summer route from the Upper Trailhead is a hike/scramble that does not typically require rope or ice axe. Winter/early-season conditions require ice axe and crampons for a steep snow chute to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: Southeast-facing snow chute is an avalanche funnel, sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
Very popular trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on the route; carry all you need
Aggressive, human-habituated mountain goats near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision point on this mountain is a signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, and a sign is the best fog marker there is because it does not depend on visibility beyond arm's length. At that junction the winter climbing route breaks right, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the left one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

Second test, higher: the summer trail threads a narrow notch and then crosses west-facing slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

Honest limit, and it is seasonal rather than navigational: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

approach_variants.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

approach_variants.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: The 3,900 ft merge with the upper trail is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
Southeast-facing snow chute above timberline is an avalanche funnel, prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
No water on the upper route
Aggressive, human-habituated mountain goats near the summit
approach_variants.whyThisWay: When the road to the upper lot is snowed in or gated; longer but gentler, joining the same trail about 1,000 ft up.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first test is the merge at about 3,900 ft, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take downhill to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

The decision point is the same signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the winter climbing route breaks right up the chute, the summer trail switchbacks left. Take the left.

And the same confirmations above it: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

approach_variants.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
approach_variants.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Outside summer, while snow buries the upper switchbacks and the chute holds firm snow; needs an axe and traction and carries real avalanche risk.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and the right-hand branch out of it. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

The confirming test is that the ground stops switchbacking. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

The test for whether you should be there at all, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

expect.approach: Start at the Upper Trailhead (about 3,500 ft) at the end of the spur off FS 24, which needs a Northwest Forest Pass. Trail 812 climbs at once, with stacked switchbacks for the first 0.3 mile before it merges with the lower-trailhead trail near 3,900 ft. Continue up through forest to the signed junction near timberline, about 4,500 ft, where the winter climbers' route leaves the summer trail and goes right. Follow the heavily used footpath along the north fork of Big Creek into the basin below the south-face chute, which is the base of the climb and a usual place for a first break. In early March, snow can cover the road about a mile below the lower trailhead, adding a road walk before the trail starts.

waypoints.name: Mount Ellinor Lower Trailhead
waypoints.note: The winter and spring start: from about December into May snow usually blocks the road at or just past this lot. No pass needed. Its trail joins the one from the upper lot near 3,900 ft.

waypoints.name: Mount Ellinor Upper Trailhead (NFR 24)
waypoints.directions: From US-101 at Hoodsport, take SR 119 (Lake Cushman Road) 9.3 miles to its end, turn right on FS Road 24 for 1.6 miles, then left on FS Road 2419 for 4.9 miles to the lower trailhead. Continue 1.7 miles farther and turn left on FS Road 2419-014 to the upper trailhead lot at its end, about 3,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.
waypoints.note: The usual start from about June to October, once the road has melted out; a Northwest Forest Pass is required.

waypoints.name: Mount Ellinor summit
waypoints.directions: Climb Trail #812's stacked switchbacks 0.3 mile to where the lower-trailhead trail joins at about 3,900 ft, then continue up the south ridge to the signed junction at timberline, about 4,500 ft. In summer take the trail left, switchbacking across rocky slopes and meadows through a notch to the summit; when snow fills it, most parties climb the chute to the right instead, with ice axe and traction.

set.approach: Two trailheads serve this climb. The Upper Trailhead (about 3,500 ft, at the end of the short spur off Forest Road 2419, pass required) is the usual start from roughly June through October, once the road has melted out. From about December into May the road is commonly blocked by snow at or just past the Lower Trailhead (about 2,600 ft, no pass needed), so winter and spring parties park there and add roughly 1,000 ft of climbing and a few miles to the day; in heavy snow even that lot can be out of reach and a party may have to begin at the Big Creek campground gate. The trail from the lower lot meets the one from the upper lot near 3,900 ft, so everything above is the same. Continue to the signed junction near 4,500 ft where the winter route leaves the summer trail and heads right into the basin below the chute.

before.name: Southeast Chute
before.overview: Hiking from the lower trailhead covers 6 miles. About a third of the way up, the trail opens onto an avalanche chute, long and straight, rising into the basin below the summit; from there bear SW for the true summit. Use caution on the steep chute and on the last steep section between the basin and the summit, and note abrupt ledges in nearly every direction on the summit. Early in the season the descent gives a superb glissade. Plan on 3.5 to 4 hours to the top; the climb gains about 3200ft.
watch_out: Mid-chute narrowing in April: a deep glissade trench runs down the middle; climb beside it, not in it.
By mid to late May, snow bridges and hollow voids over running water form in the chute.

before.descent_text: Descend the chute you climbed. When the snow is continuous, most parties glissade it with an axe in hand, losing roughly 1,000 ft quickly; only do so in control, because a fall on firm or icy snow, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower down, can injure. If the snow is hard near the top, face in and use crampons for the first part, and in a thaw the surface turns sloppy and post-holes. At the foot of the chute, rejoin the climbers' path through the basin to the timberline junction and follow Trail 812 down to the Upper Trailhead. Late in the season, when the snow runs out, use the summer trail.
